newsitem.title: USA: S. Carolina bills could affect public power-Nuveen.
newsitem.headline: S. Carolina bills could affect public power-Nuveen.

text.p: The South Carolina legislature is unlikely to pass sweeping proposals to deregulate electric utilities this year, but the state's two major public power issuers could be significantly affected if it does, according to a report by John Nuveen & Co Inc.
A House proposal (HB3414) calls for the complete deregulation of South Carolina's electric utility by Jan 1, 1999. A companion bill introduced in the Senate (SB346) extends the date to Dec 31, 2000.

"It is highly unlikely either bill will become law this year because most of the state's electric utilities would prefer taking a slow approach to deregulation," Nuveen vice president Jerry Lepinski said in the report.

But the report said the bills were noteworthy because of their potential impact on two major public power issuers -- the South Carolina Public Service Authority, known as Santee Cooper, and Piedmont Municipal Power Agency.
The House bill gives public utilities the option to participate in the deregulation process while the Senate bill requires their participation.

The House bill calls for the state Public Service Commission to adopt a restucturing plan that addresses transition issues such as rate certainty, appropriate regulatory approvals, legislative intent and public comment.

It requires electric utilities to file with the PSC their own restructuring ideas that address topics such as recovery of stranded costs, transmission and distribution policy, customer choice and unbundling of services.

If enacted, the House bill would also affect areas dominated by the state's three major investor-owned utilities -- Duke Power Co, South Carolina Electric & Gas Co, and Carolina Power & Light Co, Nuveen said.
The legislation is expected to result in substantial savings to customers, reducing residential rates by as much as 20 percent because of increased choice, Nuveen said.

Neither bill fully addresses an electric utility's obligation to serve a customer who switched providers and subsequently decided to return to its orignial provider, Nuveen said. Neither does anything to ensure continued reliability, Nuveen said.

The Senate bill addresses the tax implications of deregulation but the House bill does not, Nuveen said. The Senate bill requires the state to assess the amount of state and local tax revenue derived from previously regulated electric suppliers that will enter the competitive market and note how revenues to each state or local government entity are changed by restructuring to competition.
New rules and assessements to differenc classes of power suppliers would be required, Nuveen said.

Under the bills' reciprocity provisions, no competitor must be allowed access to a utility's customers unless comparable and reciprocal access is provided to that competition's customers, Nuveen said.
South Carolina has about 40 public power suppliers, 10 of which are members of and participants in the Piedmont Municipal Power Agency.

Its other public power supplier, Santee Cooper, sells energy, primarily at wholesale, to various customers including a generation and transmission cooperative that in turn serves 15 rural distribution cooperatives in 35 of the state's 46 counties.
Santee Cooper has $2.4 billion of bonds outstanding, serves over half of the state's electric customers and charges rates that are very competitive, Nuveen said.

It plans to pay down as much debt as possible by 2000 to further enchance its competitive position. With nuclear power accounting for only 13 percent of its fuel mix, stranded costs should not be as great as for neighboring utilities, Nuveen said.

"Overall the outlook for South Carolina Public Service Authority is stable even with the enactment of legislation calling for full deregulation of South Carolina's electric utility industry," Nuveen said.
Piedmont Municipal Power Agency has $1.3 billion of bonds outstanding, and its wholesale charge to its 10 participants are comparatively high, Nuveen said.
"PMPA has developed a plan to reduce its bulk power charges. However, the plan's timetable may be too long if the state implements deregulation in the near future," Nuveen said.
"Fortunately, investor-owned utilities are not pushing for immediate deregulation," Nuveen said.

The report concludes that if state legislation is delayed and no federal legislation is passed, the publicly owned utilities will enough time to "make adjustments to their overall city and enterprise operations."
